plain: In Southern states, about 42 out of every 100 eligible people voted. Everywhere else it was about 50 out of 100. This gap shows up no matter how we slice the data, so it's very unlikely to be a fluke. The data can't tell us why, though.
title: Southern states turned out 7.7 points lower than the rest of the country
explanation: The 17 Southern jurisdictions averaged 42.1% VEP turnout versus 49.8% for the other 34. Census region alone accounts for 26% of the between-state variance (ANOVA p = 0.002); the other three regions do not differ significantly from each other (ANOVA p = 0.917). After adjusting for every other available variable the gap is -7.2 points (p = < 0.001).
why_interesting: It is the largest and most stable pattern in the file: it survives every specification tried (100% of 128 models, across both outcomes and four samples, significant in the same direction). Because 'South' is a bundle of many state characteristics, it is a pointer to explanations rather than an explanation.

stats.test: Welch t-test; Mann-Whitney U; bootstrap CI for difference

hypotheses: Electoral competitiveness: 2022 turnout tends to be higher where statewide races are close and heavily contested; many Southern states had lopsided statewide contests. (Not testable here: the file has no race-margin or spending data.)

Election administration: states differ in registration deadlines, same-day registration, mail-ballot rules, and polling-place access. Several of the highest-turnout states are known for permissive registration or all-mail voting. (Not testable here.)
Population composition: education, income, age and residential stability are strong individual-level predictors of voting and differ by region. (Not in the dataset.)
Historical and institutional legacies of voting restrictions in the South may persist in political participation norms and party organisation.
alternatives: Measurement: 5 of the 17 Southern jurisdictions use a highest-office numerator, which understates total ballots.
adjust_alt
Classification: DC is in the Census 'South' but is an atypical, fully urban jurisdiction.
exclude_dc
Confounding by incarceration: Southern states imprison a larger share of adults.
adjust_prison
A few extreme states (e.g., Mississippi, Tennessee) could drive the mean gap.
rank_test
limitations: Region is an external label, not a mechanism: the data cannot say which Southern characteristic matters.
51 aggregate observations: state-level patterns do not describe individual voters (ecological fallacy).
One election (a midterm). The gap may differ in presidential years or other midterms.
verdict_rule: Welch p < 0.05, adjusted p < 0.05, and ≥ 80% of VEP specifications significant in the same direction
confidence_plain: We're confident this pattern is real.

plain: How you count matters! If you divide votes by all adults (including people who aren't allowed to vote, like non-citizens), states with many immigrants look like they vote less. Divide by only the people who can legally vote and most of that difference disappears. CA drops 10 places in the ranking just from this choice.
title: Measuring turnout against all adults manufactures a 'non-citizen' penalty
headline_stat: r(non-citizen, VAP rate) = -0.29 vs r(non-citizen, VEP rate) = -0.11
explanation: With the VAP denominator, states with more non-citizens look like lower-turnout states (r = -0.29, p = 0.039). With the VEP denominator, which removes people who cannot legally vote, the association weakens to r = -0.11 (p = 0.426). The VEP−VAP difference in turnout tracks non-citizen share almost perfectly (r = 0.93). CA falls 10 places in the ranking when VAP is used.
why_interesting: This is a cautionary measurement result: a researcher who used the more commonly published VAP rate would 'find' an immigrant-share effect that is largely an accounting consequence of counting ineligible residents in the denominator.
hypotheses: Mechanical: non-citizens are in VAP but cannot vote, so VAP-based turnout falls by roughly the non-citizen share even if every eligible citizen behaved identically.
Any residual association under VEP could reflect real differences (for example, newly naturalised citizens or mixed-status communities voting at different rates), but the data cannot isolate this.
alternatives: Non-citizen share is itself an estimate (survey-based), so VEP inherits its error; a state with an overestimated non-citizen share gets an inflated VEP rate.
Non-citizen share correlates with state size, so size could mask or mimic the relationship.
adjust_size
limitations: VEP itself is an estimate built from the very variables tested here; errors in non-citizen counts flow straight into the outcome.
Cannot separate the voting behaviour of naturalised citizens from that of native-born citizens.
verdict_rule: Non-citizen association significant with VAP outcome (p < 0.05) but not with VEP outcome
confidence_plain: The pattern comes from how turnout is measured.

plain: States that imprison more people have somewhat lower turnout. But many of those states are in the South, which votes less for other reasons. Once we take the South into account, the link gets 52% weaker and could just be chance.
title: States with more people in prison vote less, but being in the South explains about 52% of that
headline_stat: r = -0.34 (BH q = 0.053); slope -13.2 → -6.3 after adjusting for South
explanation: Each additional percentage point of adults in prison is associated with -13.2 points lower VEP turnout (r = -0.34, p = 0.013, bootstrap 95% CI for r -0.58 to -0.08). But Southern states imprison more people (point-biserial r = 0.41), and with a South indicator in the model the slope falls to -6.3 (p = 0.192). Within the South (r = -0.23) and outside it (r = -0.15) the association is weaker and not significant. After Benjamini-Hochberg correction for testing 8 predictors, q = 0.053 (not significant at 0.05).
why_interesting: A textbook confounding pattern: a plausible-sounding bivariate link that largely reflects a shared regional pattern. Note that prisoners are already removed from VEP, so this is not a mechanical denominator effect.
hypotheses: Spillover: high incarceration may depress participation among family and community members of people who are incarcerated (a hypothesis from the political-science literature; not testable with state aggregates).
Common cause: state political culture, poverty, and policy regimes could drive both incarceration and turnout.
alternatives: Regional confounding (South has both higher incarceration and lower turnout).
adjust_south
Influential states (DC has 0 prisoners because DC felons are held federally).
exclude_dc
Outcome choice: is the pattern the same with the VAP rate?
vap_outcome
limitations: State prison counts only; federal prisoners and jail populations are not broken out.
Cross-sectional: cannot establish whether incarceration affects turnout, or vice versa, or neither.
verdict_rule: Bivariate p < 0.05 but p ≥ 0.05 once South is controlled
confidence_plain: Another factor seems to be behind this.

plain: One fancier model hints that states with more non-citizens vote a bit less once you account for state size and region. But small, reasonable changes to the analysis make it disappear, so we don't trust it. Think of it as a hunch, not a finding.
title: A hidden non-citizen/size pattern appears in multivariable models, but it is fragile
headline_stat: Adjusted coef = -0.59 pts per point (p = 0.070); bootstrap 95% CI -1.24 to 0.02
explanation: Alone, neither non-citizen share (r = -0.11) nor state size (r = -0.01) predicts VEP turnout. Because they are correlated with each other (r = 0.50), adjusting for size and South makes non-citizen share look negative (-0.59 per point, p = 0.070) and size look positive (3.43 per tenfold increase, p = 0.122). Among VEP-outcome specifications only 34% are significant in that direction, and dropping single states moves p across 0.05 (7 of 51 leave-one-out fits are significant).
why_interesting: A 'suppressor' pattern like this is exactly what an automated search would surface as a discovery. Showing that it depends on model choices is the point: treat it as a hypothesis for other data, not a finding.
hypotheses: If real, large states with smaller immigrant populations (e.g., in the industrial Midwest) might combine high organisational/campaign intensity with fewer barriers for newly naturalised voters.
More likely, it is a statistical artefact of conditioning on two correlated variables in a small sample.
alternatives: Overfitting: with 51 observations and several candidate controls, some specifications will cross p < 0.05 by chance.
spec
Specific states (California, New Jersey) may drive the adjusted coefficient.
loo
limitations: Not pre-registered; found by searching many models, so nominal p-values overstate the evidence.
verdict_rule: Bootstrap 95% CI includes 0, or < 80% of VEP specifications significant

plain: 12 states only report votes for the top race on the ballot, not every ballot cast. That makes their turnout look a little lower than it really was. They average 3.4 points lower, but a gap that small could be chance.
title: 12 states are measured differently and average 3.4 points lower
explanation: For AL, ID, KS, MS, MO, OK, PA, RI, SD, TN, TX, WI, the CSV footnote says the numerator is votes for the highest office (or a ballot measure) rather than total ballots cast. Those states average 44.6% vs 48.0% for the rest. The gap is not statistically significant (Welch p = 0.221; -2.6 pts after adjusting for South, p = 0.214), but its direction matches what under-counting would produce.
why_interesting: Highest-office votes exclude ballots that skip that race, so these 12 rates are lower bounds. Of the five lowest-turnout states, 3 are * states (MS, TN, AL), so comparisons at the bottom of the ranking are partly comparisons of measurement methods.
hypotheses: Roll-off: some voters skip the top race, so highest-office counts sit a little below total ballots.
These states may also differ substantively (most are Southern or Midwestern), so the gap mixes measurement and real differences.
alternatives: Region confounds the comparison.
adjust_south
limitations: The size of each state's undercount is unknown from this file.
verdict_rule: Difference not significant (p ≥ 0.05); flagged because of the known measurement difference
confidence_plain: A quirk in how some states count.

plain: Whether a state bars people with felony convictions from voting doesn't seem to change its overall turnout much. But very few states fall into some of the groups, so we can't be sure.
title: How broadly a state disenfranchises people with felonies shows no clear link to turnout
explanation: Grouping states by whether they disenfranchise no one, only prisoners, or also people on probation or parole gives means of No felony disenfranchisement 52.5% (n=3), Prison + probation/parole 46.0% (n=27), Prison only 48.0% (n=21). Differences are not significant (ANOVA p = 0.270). The share disenfranchised while on probation or parole is also unrelated (r = -0.11, p = 0.459).
why_interesting: The regime is derived from the data itself (zero probation/parole counts), but only 3 jurisdictions disenfranchise no one, so power is very low.
hypotheses: Disenfranchised populations are a small share of adults (at most a few percent), so effects on aggregate turnout would be small even if real.
alternatives: The 'no disenfranchisement' group contains only DC, ME, VT.
limitations: Regime is inferred from counts, not from statutes; small groups give low power.
verdict_rule: ANOVA and Kruskal-Wallis p ≥ 0.05, and probation/parole share p ≥ 0.05

plain: Big states and small states vote at about the same rate. Size just doesn't seem to matter.
title: State size has essentially no relationship with turnout
explanation: Large and small states turn out at similar rates (Pearson r = -0.01, Spearman ρ = 0.05; quadratic term p = 0.676). The confidence interval rules out strong relationships (|r| above about 0.28). Even so, weighting by population matters for the national figure: the unweighted state mean is 47.2% while the national rate is 46.2%.
why_interesting: A useful null: theories that small states vote more (stronger civic ties) or less (fewer competitive races) find no support at this level.
hypotheses: Large and small states each contain both competitive and uncompetitive environments, which may cancel out.
alternatives: Size could matter within regions even if not overall.
within_region
limitations: A null in 51 units cannot rule out modest effects (see the CI).

plain: Even using everything in this file, we can only predict about 25% of why states differ. Things not in this data, like close races, voting rules, or who lives in each state, probably matter a lot.
title: Most of the 30-point spread in turnout is not explained by anything in this file
explanation: Turnout ranges from 32.5% (MS) to 62.3% (OR). A model with every available characteristic fits R² = 0.43 in-sample, but predicts held-out states with R² = 0.25. The South indicator alone gets 0.20 out-of-sample. The remaining variation must come from factors outside this dataset.
why_interesting: Sets expectations: this dataset describes turnout and eligibility well, but it was not designed to explain turnout.
hypotheses: Likely candidates outside the file: race competitiveness, campaign spending, mail and registration rules, education, age structure.
limitations: Out-of-sample R² with n = 51 is itself noisy.
verdict_rule: Leave-one-out R² of the full model < 0.5
confidence_plain: Most of the story isn't in this data.
